q: This is the study of past human societies through their physical remains, such as tools, pottery, and buildings. Practitioners dig at sites using trowels and careful grids. Howard Carter and Heinrich Schliemann practiced it. For 10 points, name this field.

Archaeologists record exactly where in the ground each of these is found, since its context tells as much as the thing itself. Examples include a stone arrowhead, a clay pot, or a coin made by people in the past. Unlike a fossil, it was made or shaped by humans. For 10 points, give this term for a human-made object studied for clues about the past.

This skeleton of an Australopithecus afarensis, discovered in Ethiopia in 1974 by Donald Johanson, is about three million years old. It was named after a Beatles song. For 10 points, give the name of this famous hominid fossil.

This married couple of paleoanthropologists found fossils of early humans at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania. Their son Richard also became a famous fossil hunter. For 10 points, give the surname of this family.

This species of early human lived in Europe and western Asia in the Ice Age and made stone tools. It is known from the type site in a German valley and is now extinct, though many people today carry a few of its genes. For 10 points, name this relative of our species.

This species, whose name means upright man, lived from about 1.9 million years ago and was the first to leave Africa. Its members used fire and made hand axes. For 10 points, name this species of early human.

Remains of this species dating to about 300,000 years ago have been found at Jebel Irhoud in Morocco. Along with Neanderthals and Denisovans, it was one of several human groups alive in the Ice Age. It is the only surviving member of the genus Homo. For 10 points, give the Latin name, meaning wise man, of modern humans.

This German-born American founded American anthropology and taught at Columbia. He argued against racial theories and promoted cultural relativism. For 10 points, name this man who studied the Kwakiutl.
This American anthropologist wrote Coming of Age in Samoa in 1928. She studied cultures in the Pacific, including New Guinea, and became a popular public figure. For 10 points, name this woman.

This Polish anthropologist pioneered fieldwork by living among the Trobriand Islanders. He wrote Argonauts of the Western Pacific. For 10 points, name this man who made participant observation central to ethnography.

This prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in England consists of a circle of huge standing stones. It may have been used for ceremonies, and its builders moved stones from Wales. For 10 points, name this site.

Chemical and DNA studies have suggested this ruler's death at about age nineteen involved an infection and a broken leg. His tomb was found in 1922 by Howard Carter in the Valley of the Kings and contained a golden death mask. His father may have been Akhenaten. For 10 points, name this boy king of Egypt.
This Roman city near Naples was buried by ash from Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. Excavations have revealed homes, shops, and the casts of its residents. For 10 points, name this preserved city.
This Inca site in the Andes of Peru, built in the 1400s, was rediscovered by Hiram Bingham in 1911. It is high on a mountain ridge above the Urubamba River. For 10 points, name this lost city.

This method of dating organic remains measures the decay of an unstable isotope with a half-life of about 5,700 years. Willard Libby developed it. For 10 points, name this technique, which uses an isotope of an element found in all living things.

This kind of anthropological study involves extended fieldwork and writing a detailed description of a particular culture. The word combines the Greek roots for people and writing. For 10 points, name this research method.

This is the belief that a culture should be understood on its own terms rather than judged by outside standards. Franz Boas championed it. For 10 points, name this idea, which is the opposite of ethnocentrism.

This word names the way people in a society are related by blood, marriage, or adoption, as in clans and extended families. Anthropologists draw charts to show these ties. For 10 points, name this concept.
These societies obtain food by gathering wild plants and hunting animals rather than farming. The San of southern Africa and the Inuit are examples. For 10 points, name this kind of society.

Around 10,000 years ago, people in the Fertile Crescent began to farm and domesticate animals, leading to permanent villages. V. Gordon Childe gave this name to the change. For 10 points, name this transition from foraging to agriculture.
These early modern humans lived in Europe about 40,000 years ago and painted animals on cave walls. They are named for a rock shelter in southwestern France. For 10 points, name this group.

Most of these were carved from volcanic tuff at the Rano Raraku quarry, and some wear red topknots. They stand on stone platforms called ahu. They were made by the Polynesian Rapa Nui people. For 10 points, name these large stone figures with oversized heads found on Easter Island.

Workers' villages found near them show that the builders were paid laborers rather than slaves. The earliest, at Saqqara, was designed for Djoser by Imhotep as a stepped structure. The largest, built for Khufu, was the tallest human-made structure for thousands of years. For 10 points, name these tombs of the pharaohs near Giza.
This Mesoamerican civilization built Chichen Itza and Tikal, developed a calendar, and used a writing system of glyphs. It flourished in Yucatan and Guatemala. For 10 points, name this civilization.

Canadian authorities banned this ceremony from 1885 to 1951 because they saw it as wasteful. Hosts of this Pacific Northwest ceremony give away blankets, copper, and food to guests to gain status. Franz Boas and Ruth Benedict wrote about it. For 10 points, name this feast and gift-giving event.

Captain James Cook brought this word into English after visiting Tonga in the eighteenth century. Sigmund Freud wrote a book about it in 1913. Examples include avoiding certain names of the dead and the near-universal ban on incest. For 10 points, give this term for a strong social prohibition.
This anthropologist wrote Patterns of Culture, comparing the Zuni, Kwakiutl, and Dobu. She also wrote The Chrysanthemum and the Sword about Japan. For 10 points, name this student of Franz Boas.

This thinker's Elementary Structures of Kinship analyzed marriage exchange, and he proposed that myths are built of binary oppositions like raw and cooked. He spent time with the Nambikwara and Bororo in Brazil before returning to France. For 10 points, name this anthropologist, the founder of structural anthropology.

The Haida, Tlingit, and Kwakwaka'wakw carve these from tall cedar trees. They show animals such as the raven, eagle, and bear that serve as clan crests and illustrate family stories. They are not objects of worship, despite the name. For 10 points, name these tall carved wooden monuments of the Pacific Northwest, sometimes called by a word for a clan emblem.

These enormous drawings of a hummingbird, a monkey, and a spider were made in the Peruvian desert by removing dark stones to reveal lighter ground. They were made by the Nazca culture about two thousand years ago and are best seen from the air. For 10 points, name these giant geoglyphs, named for a Peruvian plain.

q: The founders of this field in the nineteenth century compared Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin and found regular sound changes. Subfields include phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics. Ferdinand de Saussure and Noam Chomsky shaped it in the twentieth century. For 10 points, name this scientific study of language.

Latin grammarians called this part of speech by a word meaning name. It can be common, like city, or proper, like Paris. Words of this kind can also be singular or plural, and they often follow the words a, an, and the. For 10 points, name this part of speech that names a person, place, thing, or idea.

Linguists classify these as transitive, intransitive, or linking, depending on whether they take objects. They change form to show tense, such as walk, walked, and will walk. Auxiliary ones like have and be help form complex tenses. For 10 points, name this part of speech that expresses action or being.

Noam Chomsky's 1957 book on this subject introduced the sentence Colorless green ideas sleep furiously to show that a sentence can be correct in form but meaningless. It studies word order and how phrases are built, such as in subject-verb-object order. For 10 points, name this branch of grammar dealing with sentence structure.

Latin versions were taught for centuries to teach students how to read Cicero. The prescriptive kind tells people what is correct, while the descriptive kind records how people actually speak. It covers rules for word order, agreement, and tense, and it is often learned alongside spelling. For 10 points, name this system of rules for a language.

The word cats has two of these, and the word unbreakable has three. Some, like the prefix un, cannot stand alone and are called bound, while others, like cat, are free. Linguists identify them when analyzing how words are formed. For 10 points, name this smallest meaningful unit of language, larger than a phoneme.

English has about forty-four of them, and different languages have different inventories. The two sounds at the start of pit and bit are different ones in English, but the l and r sounds are not distinguished in Japanese. For 10 points, name this smallest unit of sound that distinguishes meaning, studied in phonology.
This term is used for a regional or social variety of a language that differs in vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation. Southern American English is an example. For 10 points, name this term.

This American linguist wrote Syntactic Structures in 1957 and proposed that humans have an innate capacity for grammar. He taught at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. For 10 points, name this man.

This large family of languages includes English, Spanish, Hindi, and Russian. It was reconstructed by comparing words across languages. For 10 points, name this language family, spoken from Europe to India.
This is a set of letters used to write a language. The English one has twenty-six letters. The word comes from the first two letters of the Greek one. For 10 points, name this term.

Julius Caesar and Cicero wrote in this language, which was spread by the Roman Empire. Medieval scholars used it for scholarship, and the Catholic Church used it for liturgy for centuries. It evolved into the Romance languages and gave English words such as agriculture and senate. For 10 points, name this language of ancient Rome.

This language has a regular grammar with no exceptions, and its nouns end in o and its adjectives in a. It was first published in 1887 under the pseudonym of a doctor whose name meant one who hopes. Some people speak it as a native tongue today. For 10 points, name this constructed language created by L. L. Zamenhof.

This term describes a simplified language that develops between groups with no common language, usually for trade. When it becomes the first language of children, it is called a creole. For 10 points, name this term.

Haitian one is based on French and spoken by most people in Haiti, while Gullah is spoken on the coast of South Carolina and Georgia. Tok Pisin, in Papua New Guinea, started as a trade language and later became the first language of many speakers. For 10 points, name this kind of language that arises from the mixing of languages and becomes a native tongue.

Linguists study how vowels shift in cities such as Boston and New York, and the Northern Cities Vowel Shift changed the pronunciation of many words. Unlike dialect, this term does not include differences in grammar or vocabulary. For 10 points, name this characteristic way that people from a region pronounce words.

New examples are often created by teenagers and spread by music and social media. The word skedaddle and the phrase cool cat were once examples of it, and many expressions later enter standard dictionaries. It is more casual than formal speech. For 10 points, name this kind of informal vocabulary used among peers.

Words such as sizzle, hiss, and boom are of this kind, and comic books are full of them. The word itself comes from Greek roots meaning name making. In different languages, the same animal sounds are written differently, as with English woof and Japanese wan. For 10 points, name this word-formation process in which a word imitates a sound.

The English words rewrite, unhappy, and disagree each have one of these. Latin and Greek supplied many of them, such as pre, sub, and anti. Unlike a suffix, it comes before the root. For 10 points, name this group of letters added to the front of a word to change its meaning.

In English, words like happiness, teacher, and quickly show common ones. They can change a word's part of speech, as when adding ly turns an adjective into an adverb. Inflectional ones like s and ed change tense or number. For 10 points, name this group of letters added to the end of a word.

The International Phonetic Alphabet arranges them on a chart by tongue height and frontness. In English they are written with the letters a, e, i, o, and u, and sometimes y. Their sounds are produced without closing the mouth or throat. For 10 points, name these speech sounds made with an open vocal tract.

English has about twenty-four of them. They are classified by where in the mouth they are made, such as the lips or the teeth, and how, such as a stop or a fricative. Letters like b, d, and k represent them. For 10 points, name these speech sounds made by blocking or narrowing the airflow.

This hypothesis, named for two American linguists, holds that the language we speak influences how we think. Benjamin Lee Whorf studied Hopi. For 10 points, name this hypothesis, named for Whorf and his teacher Edward.

Brain studies suggest that people who regularly use two languages may switch easily between tasks. Switching between languages in the middle of a conversation is called code-switching. This condition is common in places like Quebec, Wales, and Switzerland. For 10 points, name this term for being able to speak two languages fluently.

This is the main language of the Deaf community in the United States and Canada. It uses hand shapes, movement, and facial expressions, and has its own grammar. For 10 points, name this language, abbreviated A-S-L.

This Swiss linguist's students published his Course in General Linguistics, which distinguished the signifier from the signified. He is a founder of structural linguistics. For 10 points, name this man.

Linguists in this field study how a word like bank can mean a river's edge or a place for money. They also study how meaning is built up from parts, and how a sentence can be true or false. It differs from syntax in focusing on meaning, not form. For 10 points, name this branch of linguistics devoted to meaning.

The Oxford English Dictionary gives these histories for each word it lists. The word salary, for instance, goes back to the Latin word for salt, and the word muscle goes back to a Latin word for little mouse. For 10 points, name this field that studies the origin and development of words.

A thesaurus is a book that lists these. Examples include big and large, or begin and start, although few pairs of them mean exactly the same thing in every context. Writers use them to avoid repeating words. For 10 points, name these words that have the same or nearly the same meaning.

Examples include hot and cold, up and down, and love and hate. Linguists distinguish gradable pairs, such as tall and short, from complementary ones, such as alive and dead. A thesaurus often lists them. For 10 points, name these words that have opposite meanings.

q: This explorer was killed in the Philippines in 1521 by warriors of Lapulapu. His expedition continued under Juan Sebastian Elcano and completed the first voyage around the world. A strait at the southern tip of South America bears his name. For 10 points, name this Portuguese explorer who sailed for Spain.

This man led the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire, arriving in Mexico in 1519. He allied with Tlaxcalan warriors and was aided by an interpreter named Malinche. He captured the city of Tenochtitlan after the death of Montezuma II. For 10 points, name this Spanish conquistador.

This conquistador captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532. He demanded a room filled with gold and silver as ransom, then had the emperor executed. He later founded the city of Lima. For 10 points, name this Spanish conqueror of Peru.

This man led independence movements in Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, which was named for him. Nicknamed "the Liberator," he dreamed of uniting South America as Gran Colombia. He fought Spanish forces at the Battle of Boyaca. For 10 points, name this Venezuelan general.

This island nation was the site of a slave revolt that began in 1791 on the French colony of Saint-Domingue. A former slave named Toussaint Louverture became a leader of that rebellion. Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared independence in 1804. For 10 points, name this first Black-led republic in the Americas, whose capital is Port-au-Prince.

This waterway was built across Central America and opened in 1914. Workers had to fight yellow fever and malaria, and the United States took over the project after a French effort failed. A system of locks lifts ships above sea level. For 10 points, name this canal that connects the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

This Italian-born explorer sailed in 1492 with the Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria. He believed he could reach Asia by sailing west, and funding came from Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain. He landed in the Bahamas on his first voyage. For 10 points, name this explorer.

This Norse explorer, son of Erik the Red, is believed to have reached a place he called Vinland around the year 1000. The remains of a Viking settlement have been found at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. He sailed from Greenland. For 10 points, name this Icelandic-born Viking who reached North America centuries before Columbus.

This pilot disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in 1937 while trying to fly around the world. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean. Her navigator on the final flight was Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this American aviator.

These two brothers from Dayton, Ohio, made the first powered airplane flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. They ran a bicycle shop and built the Wright Flyer. Their first flight lasted only twelve seconds. For 10 points, name these brothers, Orville and Wilbur.

This mission in July 1969 landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility. Michael Collins stayed in orbit while two crewmates walked on the surface. Neil Armstrong said "one small step for man" during it. For 10 points, name this NASA mission that first landed humans on the Moon.

In 1957 the Soviet Union launched this object, the first artificial satellite, into orbit. It was a metal sphere that sent out radio beeps for weeks. Its launch alarmed the United States and began the space race. For 10 points, name this satellite whose name is the Russian word for "traveler."

This ocean liner struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic in April 1912 on its maiden voyage from Southampton. Its lack of enough lifeboats meant more than 1,500 people died. It was called unsinkable before the disaster. For 10 points, name this British ship.

This document was sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215 after English barons rebelled. It limited the power of the monarch and promised that even a king must obey the law. Its name is Latin for "Great Charter." For 10 points, name this English document.

This German goldsmith introduced movable-type printing to Europe in the 1450s. His most famous work was a Bible printed in the city of Mainz. His invention helped spread ideas during the Renaissance and the Reformation. For 10 points, name this inventor of the printing press.

This civilization built the city of Tikal and carved stone monuments in the jungles of Guatemala and the Yucatan. They had a calendar system and a written script using hieroglyphs. They played a ball game with a rubber ball. For 10 points, name this Mesoamerican civilization whose pyramids include Chichen Itza.

This empire built a network of roads through the Andes and used knotted cords called quipus to keep records. Its capital was Cusco, and its emperor was called the Sapa Inca. Machu Picchu is a famous site built by it. For 10 points, name this South American empire conquered by Pizarro.

This Aztec capital was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and connected to the shore by causeways. Its Templo Mayor honored the gods Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc. Floating gardens called chinampas fed its people. For 10 points, name this city that stood on the site of modern Mexico City.

This Venetian merchant traveled to the court of Kublai Khan in China in the thirteenth century. He described his adventures in a book dictated to Rustichello in a Genoese prison. His account introduced many Europeans to the wonders of Asia. For 10 points, name this traveler.

This wall, which divided a German city from 1961, was built by East Germany to stop people from fleeing to the West. Checkpoint Charlie was a famous crossing point. President Reagan challenged Soviet leader Gorbachev to tear it down. For 10 points, name this barrier that fell in 1989.

In October 1962 the United States discovered that the Soviet Union was placing nuclear missiles on this island. President Kennedy ordered a naval quarantine around it. The crisis ended when Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. For 10 points, name this Caribbean island led by Fidel Castro.

This Polish-born scientist won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry. She discovered the elements polonium and radium with her husband Pierre. She coined the term "radioactivity." For 10 points, name this woman, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.

In 1796 this English doctor tested a vaccine by using material from cowpox on a boy named James Phipps. His method protected people against a deadly disease that was later eradicated worldwide. He took his idea from observing milkmaids. For 10 points, name this developer of the first smallpox vaccine.

This Jewish girl hid with her family in a secret annex in Amsterdam during World War II. Her diary was published after the war by her father Otto. She died in the Bergen-Belsen camp in 1945. For 10 points, name this author of a famous diary.

This woman was the last reigning monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaii. Her government was overthrown in 1893 by American businessmen backed by United States Marines. She wrote the song "Aloha Oe." For 10 points, name this Hawaiian queen.

This French explorer made voyages to North America in the 1530s and claimed Canada for France. He sailed up the Saint Lawrence River to the Iroquoian town of Hochelaga. Native guides had told him of a place they called "kanata." For 10 points, name this explorer.

This statue-building culture on Rapa Nui carved huge stone heads from volcanic rock. Known as moai, the statues face inland from platforms. The island lies in the Pacific Ocean, belongs to Chile, and was named for the day Europeans found it. For 10 points, name this island.

This 1840 agreement between the British Crown and many Maori chiefs created a British colony in New Zealand. It was signed at a place in the Bay of Islands. Differences between the English and Maori texts caused disputes later. For 10 points, name this treaty.

In December 1911 this Norwegian explorer led the first expedition to reach the South Pole. He beat Robert Falcon Scott by about a month using sled dogs. Earlier he had sailed through the Northwest Passage. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1953 this New Zealand beekeeper and his Sherpa partner Tenzing Norgay became the first to reach the summit of Mount Everest. They climbed with a British expedition led by John Hunt. For 10 points, name this mountaineer, the first of the two men to step onto the summit.

In 1969 this historic music festival took place on a farm in upstate New York. It featured Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, and The Who, and drew about 400,000 people. It became a symbol of the counterculture of the 1960s. For 10 points, name this festival, named for a nearby town.

q: In a famous thought experiment from Philippa Foot, a runaway vehicle will kill five people unless a bystander pulls a lever to divert it onto a track where it will kill one person. A variant asks whether you would push a large man off a footbridge to stop it. The scenario tests the conflict between consequences and duties in moral reasoning. For 10 points, name this ethical dilemma involving a runaway rail vehicle.

This principle is named for a fourteenth-century English friar from a village in Surrey. It says that among competing explanations, the one making the fewest assumptions should be preferred. It is often summarized as "entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity." For 10 points, name this principle of simplicity, often described as a razor.

This view holds that the only thing a person can know to exist is their own mind. Critics note that it is nearly impossible to refute but also nearly impossible to live by. It makes everyone else's consciousness a matter of doubt, and its name comes from Latin words meaning "alone" and "self." For 10 points, name this extreme form of skepticism about other minds.

This philosophical position holds that life has no objective meaning, purpose, or value. Friedrich Nietzsche warned about its coming rise in Europe after "the death of God." Its name comes from the Latin word for "nothing." For 10 points, name this outlook that rejects meaning and morality.

This argument says that a rational person should live as though God exists, because the possible gain is infinite while the cost of belief is small. It appears in the unfinished Pensees, written by a French mathematician who also helped found probability theory. It is framed as a bet in which you must wager whether or not God exists. For 10 points, name this argument by Blaise Pascal.

Versions of this rule appear in many religions and in the sayings of Confucius. Jesus states it in the Sermon on the Mount as "do unto others as you would have them do unto you." It is a simple guide to ethical behavior based on reciprocity and empathy. For 10 points, name this moral principle, often described with a precious metal.

This concept in Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism says that intentional actions have consequences that shape future experience. In Hinduism, it is tied to the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth called samsara. The word comes from Sanskrit for "action." For 10 points, name this principle of moral cause and effect.

The Tao Te Ching is the central text of this Chinese philosophy and religion attributed to Laozi. It teaches wu wei, or effortless action, and living in harmony with the Way. Its symbol of balance shows yin and yang. For 10 points, name this Chinese tradition whose name comes from the word for "the Way."

This school of Mahayana Buddhism arose in China as Chan and later flourished in Japan. It emphasizes meditation, especially seated meditation called zazen, and sudden insight called satori. Teachers often give students paradoxical riddles called koans. For 10 points, name this school of Buddhism, which shares its name with a Japanese word for meditation.

Aristotle developed a formal system built on this type of argument with two premises and a conclusion. A standard example says: all men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal. The conclusion must follow if the premises are true. For 10 points, name this form of deductive reasoning with a major premise and a minor premise.

This 1516 book by Thomas More describes an imaginary island society with no private property and communal living. Its title is a Greek pun meaning both "good place" and "no place." The narrator, Raphael Hythloday, describes the island to More. For 10 points, name this work that gave its name to any ideal imagined society.

Philosophers debate whether humans have this capacity to choose among alternatives without being fully determined by prior causes. Compatibilists argue that it is consistent with causal determinism, while libertarians say it is not. Belief in it is often treated as a prerequisite for moral responsibility. For 10 points, name this ability to make genuine choices.

Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined a demon who knew every particle's position and could therefore predict the entire future. That thought experiment illustrates this thesis that every event is the necessary result of earlier causes. It is contrasted with the idea of free will. For 10 points, name this view that all events are causally fixed by prior conditions.

John Locke and David Hume were British proponents of this view that all knowledge comes ultimately from sense experience. It rejects the idea that the mind has innate ideas. It is usually contrasted with rationalism. For 10 points, name this theory that knowledge is based on observation and experience.

Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz are the three main figures in this seventeenth-century school of thought. Its members held that reason, rather than the senses, is the primary source of knowledge. Many accepted innate ideas and relied on mathematical deduction. For 10 points, name this philosophical school opposed to empiricism.

The study of knowledge, its nature, sources, and limits, is called this branch of philosophy. It asks how knowledge differs from mere belief and whether certainty is possible. Its name comes from the Greek word for "knowledge." For 10 points, name this branch of philosophy.

Aristotle's writings placed after his Physics gave this branch of philosophy its name. It asks what exists, such as whether there are universals or whether time is real. It studies being, causation, and the nature of reality. For 10 points, name this branch of philosophy.

Alexander Baumgarten helped name this branch of philosophy in the eighteenth century. Immanuel Kant wrote a Critique of Judgment in which he discussed the concept of the sublime. It examines the nature of beauty and art. For 10 points, name this branch of philosophy concerned with beauty and taste.

The Cartesian version of this view holds that mind and body are distinct substances. Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed the objection that it cannot explain how an immaterial mind moves a physical body. The pineal gland was Descartes's guess at the point of interaction. For 10 points, name this view that mental and physical things are fundamentally different.

Plutarch tells this puzzle about a vessel whose planks are gradually replaced one by one. The question is whether the vessel is still the same after every part has been replaced. Thomas Hobbes added a twist in which the discarded planks are reassembled into a second vessel. For 10 points, name this paradox about identity named for a legendary Athenian king.

Hilary Putnam popularized this updated version of Descartes's evil demon argument. You are imagined to be a disembodied nervous system kept alive in a nutrient bath and connected to a computer that supplies all your experiences. It asks how you could know that you are not in this situation. The Matrix is a famous film version. For 10 points, name this skeptical thought experiment about a container for an organ.

These were taught by the Buddha in his first sermon at Deer Park. They say that life involves suffering, that suffering has a cause in craving, that suffering can end, and that a path leads to its end. The path is the Eightfold Path. For 10 points, name this set of four central teachings of Buddhism.

Mohandas Gandhi, Leo Tolstoy, and Martin Luther King Jr. all advocated for this position. It is the belief that war and violence are never justified and that disputes should be settled peacefully. Gandhi linked it to the Hindu and Jain principle of ahimsa. For 10 points, name this opposition to war and violence.

Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill defended this ethical theory, which says the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. It is a form of consequentialism. Critics argue it can justify sacrificing individuals for the majority. For 10 points, name this theory of ethics.

This view holds that individuals must create their own meaning in a world without built-in purpose. It is associated with Jean-Paul Sartre, who said that "existence precedes essence." Kierkegaard is often called a forerunner. For 10 points, name this philosophy that emphasizes freedom, choice, and individual responsibility.

In this type of reasoning, a conclusion is guaranteed to be true if the premises are true and the argument is valid. A classic example moves from general rules to a specific case. It contrasts with induction, which moves from specific cases to general claims. For 10 points, name this reasoning from general principles to specific conclusions.

This type of reasoning draws general conclusions from specific observations. Seeing that the sun has risen every day and concluding that it will rise tomorrow is an example. David Hume's problem questions whether this method can ever be justified. For 10 points, name this kind of reasoning, which moves from particular cases to generalizations.

This view holds that moral judgments are true or false only relative to the standards of a culture or person. Its advocates point to the diversity of moral codes across societies. Critics say it makes it impossible to condemn practices like slavery. For 10 points, name this position opposed to universal moral standards.

Thomas Huxley coined this term in 1869 for the view that the existence of God cannot be known. It differs from atheism, which asserts that no gods exist. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning "not known." For 10 points, name this position on religion based on uncertainty.

This school of thought, founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium, held that virtue is the only good and that one should accept what one cannot control. Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus were famous adherents. The word is now used for someone who endures pain without complaint. For 10 points, name this philosophy.

The Greek philosopher who said "I know that I know nothing" asked questions that led others to examine their beliefs. He was tried in Athens in 399 BC on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth. He drank hemlock rather than flee. For 10 points, name this teacher of Plato.
Answer these questions about logical fallacies.
parts: An argument that attacks the person making a claim rather than the claim itself is called this, from Latin for "to the man."
Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is this fallacy, named for a figure made of hay.
This fallacy claims that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of extreme consequences without evidence. It is named for a type of incline.

q: Answer these questions about branches of philosophy.
parts: Which branch of philosophy studies right and wrong and how people should live?
Which branch studies the principles of valid reasoning and argument?
Which branch examines the justification of government, rights, and justice?

q: Answer these questions about Buddhism.
parts: Siddhartha Gautama is better known by what title meaning "awakened one"?
This is the state of liberation from suffering and rebirth, whose name means "blowing out" in Sanskrit.
Siddhartha attained enlightenment while meditating under a tree of what name?

q: Answer these questions about Confucianism.
parts: Who was the Chinese philosopher whose teachings emphasize family, ritual, and respect for elders?
Which collection of his sayings, compiled by his disciples, is the central text of Confucianism?
What term names the virtue of respect and care for one's parents and ancestors?

q: Answer these questions about philosophy of religion.
parts: The question of why a good and all-powerful God allows suffering is called the problem of what?
What medieval archbishop of Canterbury proposed the ontological argument, which says that God is the greatest conceivable being?
The argument that everything has a cause and so a first cause must exist is named for what branch of study of the universe?

q: Answer these questions about Hindu philosophy.
parts: What Sanskrit term refers to duty and cosmic law in Hinduism?
What term names the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth?
What term for the ultimate reality of the universe is identified with the self, atman, in Advaita Vedanta?

q: Answer these questions about theories of knowledge.
parts: Knowledge gained independently of experience, such as that two plus two equals four, is called this, from Latin for "from the earlier."
Knowledge that depends on experience is called what, from Latin for "from the later"?
The view that knowledge is impossible or that judgment should be suspended is called what?

q: Answer these questions about types of ethics.
parts: What approach to ethics, associated with Aristotle, focuses on character rather than rules or results?
What approach, associated with Kant, says that actions are right or wrong based on duties or rules?
What approach judges actions by their outcomes, with utilitarianism as the main example?

q: This moon is the most heavily cratered object in the solar system and has a bright multi-ring basin called Valhalla. It is the outermost of the four Galilean moons and has a thin carbon dioxide atmosphere. It orbits farther from its planet than Io, Europa, or Ganymede. For 10 points, name this Jovian moon whose name starts with a C.

This Venezuelan wrote the Jamaica Letter and delivered the Angostura Address. He won the Battle of Boyacá in 1819 and helped found Gran Colombia. Known as "El Libertador," he helped liberate Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia. For 10 points, name this South American revolutionary.

This ruler's lavish pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 reportedly depressed the price of gold in Cairo. He ruled over the empire of Mali and sponsored the building of the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu. For 10 points, name this wealthy West African emperor.

Led by Hong Xiuquan, who claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus, this uprising established a "Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace" with its capital at Nanjing. It lasted from 1850 to 1864 and may have killed 20 million people. For 10 points, name this civil war against the Qing dynasty.

The Treaty of Nanking ended this conflict in 1842, ceding Hong Kong to Britain. It began after the Chinese commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed chests of confiscated opium at Canton. For 10 points, name this first of two nineteenth-century wars between Britain and Qing China over the drug trade.

This Mughal emperor founded the capital Fatehpur Sikri and promoted religious tolerance by abolishing the jizya tax. He created a syncretic faith called Din-i Ilahi and was the grandfather of Shah Jahan. For 10 points, name this ruler who expanded the Mughal Empire in the 1500s.

After winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, this man was named shogun in 1603 and founded a dynasty that ruled Japan for over 250 years. He ruled from Edo and built a system that required daimyo to spend alternate years in the capital. For 10 points, name this first Tokugawa shogun.

This ruler of the Zulu kingdom reorganized his army into regiments and perfected the "buffalo horns" battle formation. He used the short stabbing spear, the iklwa, and presided over the upheaval known as the Mfecane. For 10 points, name this Zulu king who died in 1828.

Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata were leaders in this conflict, which began in 1910 against the long rule of Porfirio Díaz. It produced the Constitution of 1917, which established land reform and limits on the Church. For 10 points, name this upheaval in Mexico.

Shah Ismail I founded this state in 1501 and made Twelver Shi'ism its official religion. Under Shah Abbas the Great, it moved its capital to Isfahan and fought repeated wars with the Ottomans. For 10 points, name this Persian dynasty that ruled until 1736.

This grandson of Genghis Khan completed the conquest of the Song dynasty and founded the Yuan dynasty. His fleets twice failed to conquer Japan, destroyed in part by storms later called "kamikaze." For 10 points, name this Mongol emperor who hosted Marco Polo.

This Korean admiral used armored "turtle ships" to defeat Japanese fleets during the Imjin War. In 1597 he won the Battle of Myeongnyang with only a dozen ships against hundreds. For 10 points, name this naval hero of the Joseon dynasty.

In 1954, forces led by General Vo Nguyen Giap besieged and defeated French troops at this battle in a valley in northwestern Vietnam. It ended French colonial rule in Indochina and led to the Geneva Accords. For 10 points, name this decisive Viet Minh victory.

This Chinese revolutionary founded the Tongmenghui and proposed the Three Principles of the People. He became the provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912 after the fall of the Qing. For 10 points, name this leader, called the "Father of the Nation" on both sides of the Taiwan Strait.

Signed in 1840 by Maori chiefs and representatives of the British Crown, this document is regarded as the founding agreement of a Pacific nation. Differences between the English and Maori texts have led to long-running disputes. For 10 points, name this treaty of New Zealand, named for a place in the Bay of Islands.

This 1857 uprising began among soldiers of the British East India Company after rumors that new rifle cartridges were greased with animal fat. Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi was a leader, and Bahadur Shah Zafar was proclaimed emperor. For 10 points, name this revolt, also called the Sepoy Mutiny.

In 1930 Mohandas Gandhi walked about 240 miles to the coast to protest the British monopoly on a basic mineral. He picked up a handful of natural deposit at the end, breaking the law. For 10 points, name this protest march to Dandi, named for the commodity.

Emperor Menelik II won this 1896 battle in the Tigray highlands against an invading Italian army. It guaranteed Ethiopian independence during the Scramble for Africa and was widely celebrated across the colonized world. For 10 points, name this battle in Ethiopia.

This man led the Gold Coast to independence from Britain in 1957, making it the first sub-Saharan African colony to do so. He was the first president of Ghana and promoted Pan-Africanism. For 10 points, name this leader who was overthrown in a 1966 coup.

A group called the "Righteous and Harmonious Fists" besieged the foreign legations in Beijing in 1900 during this uprising. An Eight-Nation Alliance relieved the siege, and the Empress Dowager Cixi supported the rebels. For 10 points, name this anti-foreign uprising in Qing China.

Admiral Togo's fleet destroyed the Russian Baltic Fleet at the Battle of Tsushima in this conflict. It ended with the Treaty of Portsmouth, negotiated by Theodore Roosevelt in 1905. For 10 points, name this war between two empires over Manchuria and Korea.

In 1819 this British official signed a treaty with a local sultan to establish a trading post that became a major port. He also served as Lieutenant-Governor of Java and wrote a history of that island. For 10 points, name this founder of modern Singapore.

The Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885 recognized this man's personal control over a territory in central Africa. Millions died under a brutal rubber-collecting regime, and he was a king of Belgium. For 10 points, name this ruler of the Congo Free State.

Egypt's President Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956, leading Britain, France, and Israel to launch an attack. Pressure from the United States and the Soviet Union forced a withdrawal. For 10 points, name this crisis that marked the decline of British power.

Hernán Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies besieged this island city in 1521 after the "Noche Triste." Its ruler Montezuma II had been taken captive earlier, and it had been the capital of the Mexica people. For 10 points, name this city on a lake, now buried beneath Mexico City.

Pachacuti expanded this empire from its capital at Cusco, and its road system and quipu record-keeping linked an Andean realm. Francisco Pizarro captured its ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532. For 10 points, name this empire of Peru, centered on Machu Picchu.

This British navigator explored the Pacific on three voyages, charted New Zealand and the eastern coast of Australia, and crossed the Antarctic Circle. He was killed in a dispute with Hawaiians at Kealakekua Bay in 1779. For 10 points, name this captain of HMS Endeavour.

The Han emperor Wudi sent this explorer west to seek allies against the Xiongnu. He was held captive for about a decade, and his reports opened up what became the Silk Road. For 10 points, name this Chinese envoy to Central Asia.

This French historian of the Annales school wrote "The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II." He stressed long-term geography and the "longue durée" over political events. For 10 points, name this historian.

Don John of Austria commanded the Holy League fleet in this 1571 naval battle against the Ottomans in the Gulf of Corinth. The Spanish author Miguel de Cervantes was wounded here and lost the use of his left hand. For 10 points, name this large galley battle.

This Central Asian conqueror made Samarkand his capital and defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara in 1402. He claimed descent from Genghis Khan and is sometimes called "the Lame." For 10 points, name this founder of the Timurid Empire, also known as Tamerlane.
Answer these questions about the wars of independence in Latin America.
parts: Which Argentine general led an army across the Andes in 1817 to liberate Chile?
Which Mexican priest began the independence movement with the Grito de Dolores in 1810?
Which 1824 battle in the Andes effectively ended Spanish rule in South America?

q: Answer these questions about Chinese dynasties.
parts: Which was the last imperial dynasty of China, overthrown in 1912?
Which dynasty, founded by Zhu Yuanzhang, built the Forbidden City?
Which dynasty, under Qin Shi Huang, first unified China in 221 BC?

q: Answer these questions about African history.
parts: Which West African empire, centered on Gao under Askia Muhammad, succeeded Mali?
Which city in Ethiopia is famous for its rock-hewn churches?
Which medieval stone-walled city in southern Africa gave its name to a modern country?

q: Answer these questions about decolonization.
parts: Who led Indonesia to independence from the Netherlands and became its first president?
Who became the first president of independent Kenya?
Which North African country fought a war of independence against France from 1954 to 1962?

q: Answer these questions about the Middle East after World War I.
parts: Which secret 1916 agreement divided Ottoman Arab lands between Britain and France?
Which 1917 declaration expressed British support for a Jewish national home in Palestine?
Which Turkish leader founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923?
